title: Hubble image of Herbig-Haro object HH 110
caption: The Herbig-Haro object HH 110, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HH 110 · constellation Orion · about 1500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows Herbig-Haro 110, a geyser of hot gas streaming away from a newborn star. Herbig-Haro objects are glowing patches that form where jets of material shot out by young stars slam into the surrounding gas and dust.

HH 110 is unusual. Most Herbig-Haro objects come in pairs, marking jets that shoot out in opposite directions, but this one appears on its own. Astronomers suspect it could be the extension of a second object, HH 270, whose flow has been deflected after hitting a dense cloud of gas.

If that idea is right, HH 110 shows how the outflows of young stars can interact with their surroundings, changing course when they meet denser material. Hubble's view combines visible and infrared light, including a filter that picks out glowing hydrogen.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.58 x 2.03 arcminutes) and distance (1500 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.1 × 0.9 light-years. Its light set out about 1,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines a hydrogen-alpha filter from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with visible and near-infrared filters from Wide Field Camera 3. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared data are invisible to the eye, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hot gas in the jet.
